Empirical Research Plan:  “Life Expectancy and Economic Growth”

============================================================
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Two–stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental‐variables (IV) design, complemented by a staggered-event DID / event-study as a robustness exercise.  
Why IV?  
•	The causal regressor, life-expectancy (LE) at birth, is jointly determined with income (reverse causality) and correlated with many omitted factors (institutions, education, etc.).  
•	The post-WWII wave of global health innovations (DDT, penicillin, polio vaccine, small-pox eradication campaigns, etc.) created large, externally driven mortality reductions whose size differed systematically with countries’ PRE-intervention disease profiles. This provides exogenous, plausibly as-good-as-random variation in LE growth that is not driven by domestic economic policy.

Core instrument (“predicted life expectancy”,  PLEit):
  PLEit  =  Σd (Pre-1940 mortality share of disease d in country i) × (Global mortality decline for disease d between t–1 and t)

This is identical in spirit to Acemoglu-Johnson (2007): interaction of time-varying global mortality shocks with fixed country-level exposure weights.  It is continuous, strong and plausibly exogenous.

The DID / event-study specification (high vs. low pre-intervention disease burden) provides an intuitive visual check of parallel trends and dynamic effects.

============================================================
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable:  
 LEit  = life expectancy at birth in country i, year t (continuous, in years).  

Instrument (“treatment intensity”):  
 High-exposure countries (above the global median of infectious-disease mortality, 1938–40) receive larger shocks to PLEit after 1945.  

Control group (for DID robustness):  
 Low-exposure countries (below median pre-1940 infectious-disease mortality).  

Treatment timing / event date:  
 t0 = 1945 (first widespread release of penicillin and DDT). Event window 1945–1980 captures the bulk of mortality breakthroughs.

No running variable needed (not RDD).

============================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
1. Relevance (Cov[PLEit, LEit] ≠ 0): Global mortality shocks meaningfully move domestic LE; strongly testable in first stage. Plausible, well-documented.

2. Exclusion Restriction: PLEit affects GDP per capita (Yit) only via its impact on LE, not through other channels. Plausibility:
 •	Global health campaigns were organised by WHO/UNICEF, largely orthogonal to countries’ contemporaneous macro-policies.  
 •	Infrastructure or aid co-movements can be controlled for with country and year fixed effects (+ region×year trends).

3. Strict Exogeneity of Pre-period Exposure Weights: Pre-1940 disease structure is predetermined with respect to post-war economic shocks. Reasonable because high infectious-disease mortality was driven mainly by ecology and epidemiology, not by latent growth potential.

4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-country spillovers): One country’s mortality decline does not mechanically raise or lower another’s GDP outside general-equilibrium effects. Potentially violated via trade migration; mitigated by including region×year FEs and clustering.

5. Monotonicity (for LATE): Countries with higher pre-1940 disease weights never experience smaller exogenous LE gains when global mortality falls—highly plausible.

============================================================
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1:  Concurrent post-war aid or reconstruction programs may be larger in high-disease countries → instrument violates exclusion.  
•	Add controls for Marshall-plan eligibility, colonial status, war destruction indices.  
•	Show results robust to excluding Europe or ex-colonies.  
•	Placebo: Use pre-intervention period (1930–44) where global mortality shocks were small; estimate “effect”—should be zero.

Threat 2:  Demographic channel (LE↑ → population↑) mechanically lowers GDP per capita in short run, biasing coefficient downward; long-run effect positive.  
•	Report separate effects on GDP, GDP per worker, capital deepening, dependency ratio.  
•	Estimate distributed-lag model to trace short- vs. long-run impacts.

Threat 3:  Measurement error in historical LE (attenuation).  
•	IV naturally corrects for classical measurement error.  
•	Cross-check LE series with alternative sources (UN Demographic Yearbooks, Human Mortality Database).  
•	Instrument strength test (Kleibergen-Paap F-stat).

============================================================
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ----------------- 0. Packages -----------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # IV + fixed effects
library(did)          # for robustness DiD/event study
library(tidyverse)

# ----------------- 1. Load & Merge Data -----------------
d <- fread("country_year_health_gdp.csv")   # columns: iso, year, lifeexp, gdp_pc, pop,
                                            # diseaseX_mort_1940 (for 6–8 diseases), etc.

# ----------------- 2. Construct Instrument -----------------
# 2a. Global mortality decline by disease & year
global <- fread("global_disease_mort.csv")  # columns: year, disease, mort_rate
global <- global %>% group_by(disease) %>%
           arrange(year) %>%
           mutate(global_decline = mort_rate - lag(mort_rate))

# 2b. Wide to long merge
d_long <- melt(d,
               id.vars = c("iso","year","lifeexp","gdp_pc"),
               measure.vars = patterns("^disease"),
               variable.name = "disease",
               value.name = "mort_share_1940")

d_long <- merge(d_long, global, by = c("disease","year"))

# 2c. Predicted life expectancy change
d_long[, ple_component := mort_share_1940 * (-global_decline)]  # (-) so decline increases LE
ple <- d_long[,.(PLE = sum(ple_component, na.rm=TRUE)), by = .(iso,year)]

d <- merge(d, ple, by = c("iso","year"))

# ----------------- 3. Main 2SLS Regression -----------------
# Dep var: log GDP per capita
d[, lgdp_pc := log(gdp_pc)]

iv_main <- feols(lgdp_pc ~ lifeexp | iso + year | lifeexp ~ PLE,
                 data = d, cluster = ~iso)
summary(iv_main, cluster = "iso")

# First-stage check
fs <- feols(lifeexp ~ PLE | iso + year, data=d, cluster=~iso)
summary(fs, cluster="iso")

# ----------------- 4. Robustness: staggered DID -------------
# Define treated = high pre-1940 infectious disease mortality
cutoff <- median(d$infect_mort_1940, na.rm=TRUE)
d[, treated := (infect_mort_1940 > cutoff)]

did_data <- d[year >= 1935 & year <= 1975]
event_out <- att_gt(yname   = "lgdp_pc",
                    tname   = "year",
                    idname  = "iso",
                    gname   = "treat_year",  # first year >=1945 if treated, Inf otherwise
                    xformla = ~0,
                    data    = did_data)
ggdid(event_out)                       # event-study plot

# ----------------- 5. Save outputs -----------------
fwrite(tidy(iv_main), "results_iv.csv")
```

============================================================
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Theory suggests healthier populations accumulate more human capital, save more, and attract FDI.  However, larger surviving cohorts initially raise dependency ratios.  Net expectation:

Elasticity ≈ 0.020–0.040.  
Interpretation: a 1-year increase in life expectancy raises GDP per capita by roughly 2–4 %.  Short-run (0–5 yrs) effect may be near zero or slightly negative; medium- to long-run (10–20 yrs) strongly positive.

============================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Strong first-stage (F > 10) ………………………………… 1  
C2: Credible exclusion of instrument ………………………… 0.7  
C3: Pre-trend / parallel-trend tests via DID ……………… 0.8  
C4: No interference/SUTVA violations ……………………… 0.6  
C5: Robustness to alternative samples/specs ……………… 0.8  

Total (out of 5) ≈ 3.9.  The main lingering concern is full exclusion (C2) and possible spillovers (C4); both are partially but not fully addressable.
